title: Do Olympic ring colours stand for continents? Not individually
description: The familiar five-ring symbol hides a common quiz trap. Separate what the rings represent from what their colours mean.
practice: Try Sports Quiz for a mix of sporting questions. Keep the rings-versus-colours distinction in mind when a question sounds almost familiar.

sections.title: The tempting answer that is wrong
sections.html:
No individual Olympic ring colour is officially assigned to a particular continent. You may have seen a tidy list matching blue, yellow, black, green and red to five places. The International Olympic Committee explicitly says that interpretation is wrong.

It is an excellent quiz trap because it sounds organised and easy to learn. A neat explanation is not always the correct one.

sections.title: Read the symbol as a whole
sections.html:
The five interlaced rings represent the union of five continents and athletes meeting from across the world at the Olympic Games. The symbol expresses connection; it is not a colour-coded map.

Keep two separate questions in your head: ‘What do the rings represent together?’ and ‘Does each colour name a continent?’ The first has an answer about unity. The second has the answer no.

sections.title: Then why those colours?
sections.html:
According to the IOC, when Pierre de Coubertin created the rings in 1913, the five ring colours together with the white background covered the colours used in the national flags of the time. White is part of that explanation even though it is not a ring.

The date matters too: this is an explanation of the design at that time. Do not turn it into a new claim about every flag that exists today.

sections.title: Which statement would you trust?
sections.html:
Read these once, then choose before opening the answer.

  1. Each ring colour identifies one continent.
  2. The rings collectively express the union of five continents.
  3. The white background has no part in the colour explanation.
Check the statements

Only statement 2 is correct. Statement 1 repeats the colour-to-continent myth. Statement 3 drops the white background from Coubertin’s explanation.

If you chose 1 because you remembered a diagram from school, replace the diagram with one sentence: ‘Five rings together, not five colour labels.’ It is a smaller fact to remember, and a more accurate one.

sections.title: A useful habit for the next sports question
sections.html: When two answers both sound familiar, look for the word that changes the claim. Here it is each. In tennis it might be game versus set; in another quiz it could be first versus most. Pause on that word before choosing.
